November 2026, beschlossen, zum Gesetz zur Verbesserung der Startchancen von Kindern und zur Qualitätsentwicklung in der Kindertagesbetreuung den Vermittlungsausschuss anzurufen. Er fordert, das Gesetz grundlegend zu überarbeiten. Der Bundestag hatte das sogenannte "Startchancen- und Qualitätsentwicklungsgesetz" der Bundesregierung (21/8239(Dokument, öffnet ein neues Fenster), 21/8827(Dokument, öffnet ein neues Fenster)) am 12. November 2026 beschlossen. Kern des Gesetzentwurfs sind Vorgaben für die Feststellung des Sprach- und des Entwicklungsstands von Kindern spätestens im fünften Lebensjahr sowie zur anschließenden Förderung der Kinder. Wann der Vermittlungsausschuss zusammentritt, um das Gesetz zu beraten, steht noch nicht fest. Länderkammer: Dauerhafte Finanzierung nicht sichergestellt Wie bereits in seiner im Oktober beschlossenen Stellungnahme zum Entwurf des Gesetzes kritisiert der Bundesrat, dass der Bund den Ländern erhebliche Verpflichtungen auferlege, ohne deren dauerhafte Finanzierung sicherzustellen. Die Änderungsvorschläge des Bundesrates seien im weiteren Gesetzgebungsverfahren allenfalls punktuell aufgegriffen worden, heißt es seitens der Länderkammer zur Begründung. Die Bundesregierung habe die finanziellen Forderungen der Länder abgelehnt und entgegnet, dass im Gegenteil eher von einer Überschätzung der Kosten auszugehen sei. Eine weiterführende Untermauerung mittels einer belastbaren Kostenberechnung sei bislang jedoch ausgeblieben. Grundsatz der Veranlassungskonnexität Die Länder begründen die Anrufung des Vermittlungsausschusses damit, dass ein auf Dauer angelegtes Gesetz einer verlässlichen, dauerhaften und regelmäßig angepassten Finanzierung durch den Bund bedürfe. Im Gesetz sei jedoch nur eine auf acht Jahre begrenzte und degressive Beteiligung des Bundes vorgesehen. Diese stehe in ihrer Höhe und Dauer im Widerspruch zu den kontinuierlich anwachsenden und dauerhaft bestehenden Verpflichtungen von Ländern und Kommunen. Die Länder erinnern auch an das Prinzip der Veranlassungskonnexität, das in der gemeinsamen Besprechung der Regierungschefinnen und Regierungschefs der Länder mit dem Bundeskanzler erst vor kurzem bekräftigt worden sei. Gesetzentwurf der Bundesregierung Das Gesetz der Bundesregierung enthält eine Reihe von Regelungen zur besonderen Unterstützung von Kitas mit einem erhöhten Anteil von Kindern in herausfordernden Lebenslagen. Den betreffenden Kitas sollen zusätzliche personelle Ressourcen zur Verfügung gestellt werden. Von dieser zusätzlichen Förderung sollen mindestens zehn Prozent der Kindertageseinrichtungen in jedem Land profitieren. Für die verbindliche Feststellung des Sprach- und Entwicklungsstands der Kinder sowie für deren anschließende Förderung sollen den Kitas personelle Ressourcen für die Erhebung im Umfang von zwei Stunden je Kind sowie für die Planung und Begleitung der Förderung im Umfang von mindestens dreißig Minuten je Kind pro Woche zur Verfügung gestellt werden. Bei Kindern, die nicht in Kindertageseinrichtungen betreut werden, soll der Sprach- und Entwicklungsstand ebenfalls festgestellt und anschließend gefördert werden. Dies sollte durch Landesrecht geregelt werden. Der Bund will die Länder für die durch die Regelungen entstehenden Mehrausgaben über einen Verzicht von Einnahmen aus der Umsatzsteuer entlasten. Im parlamentarischen Verfahren wurde der Entwurf noch geringfügig geändert. So sollten die Länder mehr Flexibilität bei der Personalplanung erhalten. Der Bund will den Ländern von 2027 bis 2034 rund neun Milliarden Euro dafür zur Verfügung stellen. Allerdings sollen die Sprachstandserhebungen erst ab 2029 vollständig für alle Kinder verbindlich werden und die Tests von Motorik, Zahlenverständnis und emotionaler Entwicklung erst ab 2032. Gremium von Bundestag und Bundesrat Der Vermittlungsausschuss ist ein Gremium, das zwischen Bundestag und Bundesrat fungiert. Der Vermittlungsausschuss besteht aus 16 Mitgliedern des Bundesrates und ebenso vielen des Bundestages, die entsprechend den Fraktionsstärken benannt sind. Seine Aufgabe liegt darin, einen Konsens zwischen Bundestag und Bundesrat zu finden, wenn vom Bundestag beschlossene Gesetze im Bundesrat keine Mehrheit finden. Weichen Beschlüsse des Vermittlungsausschusses von denen des Bundestages ab, ist eine erneute Beschlussfassung im Bundestag erforderlich. Ist zu einem Gesetz die Zustimmung des Bundesrates erforderlich, so können auch der Bundestag und die Bundesregierung die Einberufung des Vermittlungsausschusses verlangen, um eine Einigung herbeizuführen. I recall that shortly after addressing this gathering in 2023, someone asked me: "Why would the Deputy President attend a business awards ceremony?" My response was simple: recognising business success goes beyond presenting trophies or celebrating financial achievement. It is about recognising men and women whose vision, hard work and willingness to take risks create opportunities for others. They create jobs, drive innovation, grow industries and contribute to the prosperity of our societies. These awards also inspire entrepreneurs, facilitate partnerships between business leaders and policymakers, and encourage investment and intra-African trade. They remind us that Africa's development cannot be driven by Governments alone. It requires strong public-private partnerships. Ultimately, the awards contribute to the aspirations of the African Union's Agenda 2063, which envisions an integrated, prosperous and peaceful Africa, driven by its own citizens. Ladies and Gentlemen, While tonight is a celebration of achievement, it is also an opportunity to reflect on the kind of Africa we are building. Our continent is experiencing economic growth and is home to some of the world's fastest-growing economies. Yet this progress coexists with persistent poverty, inequality and infrastructure deficits. The question is no longer whether Africa has potential, but whether we have the collective vision, determination and political will to translate that potential into prosperity. Africa's future must be shaped by Africans. Governments must advance regional economic integration, remove regulatory barriers and create an enabling environment for business investment and innovation. At the same time, businesses must look beyond national borders, embrace innovation and position themselves to compete in the global economy. One of the most transformative developments shaping this economy is Artificial Intelligence. AI is already driving productivity, growth and competitiveness across industries. For Africa, it presents an opportunity to address development challenges, create new industries and open up markets. We cannot afford to remain consumers of technologies developed elsewhere. We must become innovators, builders and exporters of AI solutions that respond to African realities and compete globally. Business leaders have a critical role to play. The investments you make today in AI, digital infrastructure and innovation will determine your ability to grow, create jobs and remain competitive in the economy of tomorrow. However, technology alone will not transform our continent. We must also invest in the people who will develop, adapt and deploy these technologies. Africa has the world's largest youth population, projected to exceed 830 million by 2050. By that time, the continent is expected to account for approximately 85 per cent of growth in the global workforce. This presents us with a historic demographic advantage. But it will only become a dividend if we equip young people with the necessary skills and knowledge. We must prioritise education, entrepreneurship, digital literacy and science, technology, engineering and mathematics, and prepare the youth not only to participate in the future economy, but to lead it. Ladies and Gentlemen, For Africa to realise its full potential, we need infrastructure that enables people, goods, services and ideas to move seamlessly across our continent. We need modern transport corridors, efficient ports, reliable energy systems, broadband connectivity and digital infrastructure to reduce the cost of doing business, improve competitiveness and connect our economies. This is particularly important in the context of the African Continental Free Trade Area. The AfCFTA is more than a trade agreement; it is a continental development project that offers an opportunity to transform 54 separate markets into one African market, strengthen regional value chains and ensure that more of Africa's wealth is created and processed on African soil. With a market of more than 1.4 billion people and a combined GDP exceeding US$3.4 trillion, the AfCFTA has enormous potential. According to World Bank estimates, it could increase intra-African exports by more than 80 per cent by 2035 while lifting millions of Africans out of extreme poverty. However, this promise cannot be realised through policy alone. It requires infrastructure that connects our economies and makes it easier for African businesses to trade with one another. It should not be easier, faster or cheaper to trade with markets outside our continent than with our neighbours. By investing in our people, building infrastructure and implementing the AfCFTA, we can create larger markets, attract investment, generate jobs and position Africa as a competitive force in the global economy. Ladies and Gentlemen, None of this will be achieved by Governments acting alone. It requires business leaders who are prepared to invest beyond immediate returns, embrace innovation, develop skills, build partnerships and expand into new markets. Tonight, we celebrate those who are already contributing to this vision. Through your entrepreneurship, innovation and leadership, you are creating jobs, expanding opportunities and demonstrating what is possible when African talent is given the space to thrive. Allow me to congratulate all those nominated this evening. You are the innovators, trailblazers and changemakers helping to shape the future of our continent. Whether you leave here with an award or not, continue pushing boundaries, creating opportunities and lifting others as you rise. Being recognised as a nominee is itself a remarkable achievement and reflects your commitment to excellence and contribution to economic growth and social progress. To our winners, congratulations on your achievements. May your success inspire future generations of African entrepreneurs and business leaders. May your leadership continue to advance the cause of a prosperous, integrated and globally competitive Africa. I thank you and enjoy the rest of the evening. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. Read Ambassador Greer's full letter to the Wall Street Journal below. In his op-ed “How Do You Like Those Tariffs Now?” (Nov. 11), David Hebert asserts that economists’ predictions about tariffs came true: “Americans would pay them, trading partners would retaliate, and bullying our allies would backfire.” The data tell a different story on each of these points. The first point—that American consumers bore the brunt of the tariffs—doesn’t hold up to scrutiny. Caroline Freund of the University of California San Diego published a paper in July concluding that foreign exporters absorbed roughly 40% to 50% of the 2025 U.S. tariff increases through lower export prices, “much more than earlier studies suggested.” Importers of record, typically companies, covered much of the rest. Preston Caldwell, chief U.S. economist at Morningstar, told the Journal last year that “U.S. firms are still footing most of the tariff bill, having yet to pass more than a fraction of the tariff cost on to consumers.” Nor did the tariffs trigger sweeping global retaliation. While the Trump administration put tariffs on countries all around the world, only two attempted direct retaliation: China and Canada. But in both cases, these countries eventually rolled back some of their retaliatory measures while the U.S. maintained most of its new tariffs. China has resumed buying U.S. soybeans, easing China’s leverage over U.S. farmers. As for Mr. Hebert’s argument about “backfiring,” 19 U.S. trading partners, accounting for nearly 40% of global gross domestic product, signed deals with us. In these agreements, the U.S. agreed to impose a lower tariff rate in exchange for our trading partners’ resolution of longstanding tariff and nontariff barriers—a prize free-trade fundamentalists have sought for decades. But don’t take our word for it; workers, farmers and industry leaders have praised President Trump’s deals that open foreign markets while expanding domestic jobs and investment. The U.S. has exported over $300 billion in goods and services every month this year, breaking records. We are in the tenth month of a manufacturing expansion. The economy is close to full employment. While Europe’s economic growth is sluggish and Canada’s unemployment rate rose to 6.7% in October, the U.S. is the most dynamic economy in the Group of Seven. So, yes, we like these tariffs very much. ###1d:T59e,Today, the Prime Minister, Mark Carney, met with the President of Brazil, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, on the margins of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit, in Manila, Philippines.
